Sect leader Warren Jeffs arrives in court to hear the verdict against him September 25 in St. George, Utah. In the days following the suicide attempt, while he was on suicide watch, Jeffs on separate occasions threw himself against the wall and banged his head on the wall. The day before that, Jeffs told a follower in a phone conversation that he was "covered with immorality with a sister and a daughter when I was younger." In the FLDS, members call adult women "sister," and Jeffs' meaning was unclear. Jeffs' defense attorneys, who argued against the release of the documents, said in a motion opposing the unsealing of the statements that Jeffs recanted them the following month. Defense attorneys claim Jeffs' medical condition influenced his state of mind when the statements were made. Jeffs was on the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives list when he was arrested in August 2006 outside Las Vegas, Nevada. Critics say that inside the FLDS, marriages are arranged for girls as young as 13, and competition for brides may be reduced by exiling male teens and young men. "He is a perfectly priestly man," said a woman who identified herself as Cathy. "He is a man of God, and we will always love him. Once a prophet, always a prophet." ## Background on the FLDS Church

The Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints (FLDS) is a religious sect that broke away from the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, commonly known as the Mormon Church. While the mainstream LDS Church officially abandoned the practice of polygamy in 1890, the FLDS continued to embrace plural marriage as a central tenet of their faith.

The FLDS established communities primarily in the twin border towns of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona, as well as a compound in Eldorado, Texas, known as the Yearning for Zion Ranch. Warren Jeffs assumed leadership of the church following the death of his father, Rulon Jeffs, in 2002, taking on the title of "president and prophet" and exercising near-total control over the lives of his followers.

## FBI Fugitive and Arrest

Warren Jeffs became one of the FBI's most wanted fugitives after charges were filed against him related to arranging marriages between adult men and underage girls. In May 2006, the FBI placed Jeffs on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, offering a substantial reward for information leading to his capture.

After months on the run, Jeffs was apprehended on August 28, 2006, during a routine traffic stop on Interstate 15 near Las Vegas, Nevada. Authorities discovered him traveling with cash, laptops, disguises, and other items suggesting he had been living as a fugitive.

## Trial and Legal Proceedings

Jeffs faced multiple charges across different jurisdictions. In Utah, he was initially tried as an accomplice to rape for his role in arranging a marriage between a 14-year-old girl and her 19-year-old cousin. In 2007, he was convicted, though this conviction was later overturned by the Utah Supreme Court due to faulty jury instructions.

The most significant legal proceedings occurred in Texas, where Jeffs faced charges of sexual assault of a child. In 2011, following a raid on the Yearning for Zion Ranch, Jeffs was convicted of sexually assaulting two girls, ages 12 and 15, whom he had taken as "spiritual brides." He was sentenced to life in prison plus 20 years.

## Court Documents Unsealed

Judge James Shumate, presiding over legal matters related to Jeffs in Utah, ordered the unsealing of various court documents that provided the public with insight into the internal workings of the FLDS and the allegations against its leader. These documents shed light on the church's practices, including the arrangement of underage marriages and the concentration of authority in Jeffs's hands.

The unsealed materials became important resources for understanding both the specific charges against Jeffs and the broader patterns of conduct within the FLDS community.

## Legacy

Warren Jeffs remains incarcerated in Texas, though reports have suggested he continued to attempt to lead the FLDS from behind bars. His case brought national attention to the practices of isolated religious communities and sparked ongoing discussions about religious freedom, child protection, and the limits of the law.
